title: How big should the cache be for this system?
summary: Tests whether you can size a cache from the working set (hot data), not the full dataset, and justify the number against a hit-rate target.

slides.markdown:
"How big should the cache be for this system?" is probing one specific distinction: **working set vs full dataset**. A candidate who sizes the cache to hold everything hasn't understood why caching works in the first place — a cache pays off because a small, hot slice of the data absorbs most of the traffic.

The strong answer estimates that hot slice directly, sizes the cache against it, and names the hit rate the sizing is aiming for.

Ask: **what's the access pattern** — is roughly 80% of traffic hitting roughly 20% of keys? That skew (a Pareto pattern) is common for product catalogs, social feeds, and most read-heavy systems, and it's exactly what makes caching effective at all.

If access is close to uniform instead — every key read about as often as every other — a cache sized for a small hot set won't help much, since there's no small "hot" slice to capture.

The formula: estimate the **hot working set size** (not the full dataset), and size the cache to hold it, targeting a specific **hit rate** rather than an arbitrary size.

Say the skeleton out loud before plugging in numbers: "I'd size this off the working set, not the total data, since that's the slice actually worth caching." See [caching fundamentals](caching-fundamentals) for the deeper mechanics of hit rate and working-set sizing.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: sizing the hot working set
slides.markdown:
A product catalog with 10 million items, averaging 1KB each, where 80% of traffic hits the hottest 20% of items:

```
10,000,000 items x 20% (hot fraction) = 2,000,000 hot items
2,000,000 items x 1 KB/item = 2,000,000 KB
2,000,000 KB / 1,000 = 2,000 MB = ~2 GB
```

The cache needs to hold roughly **2GB**, not the full 10GB the entire catalog would take — an 80% smaller footprint, because the working set is what actually matters.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: overhead for keys and eviction bookkeeping
slides.markdown:
Real cache usage runs higher than the raw value size — every entry also carries **key overhead** and the cache's own **eviction bookkeeping** (LRU pointers, access timestamps, hash-table slots). A reasonable rule of thumb is 20-30% on top of raw data.

Applying 30%: 2GB × 1.3 = **2.6GB**. Presenting the raw 2GB figure without this adjustment is the kind of gap that looks fine on paper and comes up short the moment the cache actually runs.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: comparing against a single node's RAM
slides.markdown:
Check the 2.6GB figure against a real machine before proposing a cluster:

```
2.6 GB (cache size) vs 32 GB (single node RAM)
2.6 / 32 ~= 8% of one node's memory
```

At roughly 8% of a single 32GB node's RAM, **one cache node comfortably suffices** for this working set — no need to reach for a distributed cache cluster before the numbers actually demand it.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: bigger cache vs diminishing returns
slides.markdown:
**Growing the cache toward the working-set size** raises the hit rate quickly — every added gigabyte captures more of the genuinely hot data. **Growing it past the working-set size** raises the hit rate much more slowly, since the additional capacity now holds increasingly cold, rarely-accessed items that barely reduce database load.

Knowing where that knee sits — roughly at the working-set size itself, here about 2.6GB — is what separates a justified cache size from a round number picked out of convenience.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how do you verify the hit rate in production?
slides.markdown:
"How do you verify this once it's live?" — instrument the cache with hit/miss counters and watch the **actual hit rate** against the target used to size it. If the real hit rate comes in well below the estimate, that's a signal the access pattern isn't as skewed as assumed, or the cache is evicting hot items too aggressively.

The estimate is a starting point, not a guarantee — production monitoring is what confirms or corrects it.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the working set doubles overnight
slides.markdown:
"A feature launch doubles the working set overnight — does your cache size still hold?" Recompute rather than assume: 2.6GB doubling to **5.2GB** is still only about 16% of a single 32GB node, so one node still comfortably suffices — the sizing survives the change without a cluster.

The answer that matters isn't "yes" or "no" on instinct, it's redoing the same working-set-vs-node-capacity check with the new number.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: sizing the cache to hold all the data "to be safe"
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** cache the full 10GB catalog instead of just the 2.6GB working set, "to be safe."

**Why it's wrong:** it 4x's the memory footprint and cost for almost no hit-rate gain, since the cold 80% of items barely gets read anyway — that memory is spent protecting against traffic that doesn't happen. It also signals a misunderstanding of why caching works at all.

**Correct model:** size to the working set and a target hit rate, verify in production, and grow only if data shows the working set itself has grown.

Compressed script: "With 10 million items at 1KB each and an 80/20 access pattern, the hot working set is about 2GB. Adding 30% for key and eviction overhead gets to 2.6GB, which is only about 8% of a single 32GB node's RAM — so one cache node suffices, no cluster needed yet. I'd verify the real hit rate once it's live and re-check if the working set grows."

Practice naming the working-set number, not the full dataset size, as your answer.
